The wise person does the same with their own life: stands upright, takes their proper position, and so gives destiny something steady to work through. A cauldron that tilts spills its contents. Get your stance and your commitments right, and what you are meant to do can take shape.

lines.text: The cauldron is turned upside down, legs in the air. It helps to tip out the stale remains. One takes a concubine for the sake of her son. No mistake.
lines.meaning: An overturned cauldron looks like a disaster, but it is the only way to empty out old, spoiled food before cooking something new. A low start can serve a purpose. The image of the concubine valued for her son says the same thing: a humble position is no bar to worth if something good comes of it. Clear out what is stale, accept an unglamorous beginning, and you have done nothing wrong.

lines.text: There is food in the cauldron. My rivals envy me, but they cannot reach me. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: You have real substance: skill, resources, something of value. That may attract jealousy or ill will from those around you. Stay focused on what you are cooking and keep your conduct correct, and their resentment will not touch you. Do not be drawn into their quarrels or defend yourself too much. Your content protects you.

lines.text: The cauldron’s ears have been changed; it cannot be lifted and moved. The fat of the pheasant goes uneaten. Rain falls, and regret passes. In the end, good fortune.
lines.meaning: You have something rich to offer, a good meal in the pot, but no one can pick it up because its handles do not fit. Your gifts are not reaching the people who could use them, perhaps because you are out of step with those in charge. Do not force it. Keep your quality, stay patient, and let things soften like rain cooling the heat. The connection will come and the waiting will end well.

lines.text: The cauldron’s legs break. The prince’s meal spills, and the one responsible is drenched in shame. Misfortune.
lines.meaning: This line holds high office near the ruler, but it leans on a weak line below and the load is too much. You may have taken on more than you can carry, or relied on helpers not up to the job. When it breaks, the failure is public and costly. This is a clear warning: check whether your supports can bear the weight, and be honest about your limits before the meal is on the floor.

lines.text: The cauldron has yellow ears and a carrying bar of gold. It pays to stay steady.
lines.meaning: This is the ruler’s line, yielding and central, at the cauldron’s ears. Yellow means the middle way; gold means strength and worth. Because you are open and receptive, capable people can take hold of you and help carry the vessel. Lead by being approachable and balanced, let others lift with you, and keep steadily to what is right.

lines.text: The cauldron has a carrying bar of jade. Great good fortune. Nothing that does not go well.
lines.meaning: Jade is hard yet gentle and warm to the touch: strength combined with grace. At the top of the hexagram, the work of nourishing others is complete and refined. You hold your influence lightly and well, and it serves everyone. This is one of the most favorable lines in the whole book. Give freely of what you have made.

life.work: Build something lasting that feeds others: a team, an institution, a craft; make sure its supports are sound and its value reaches people.
life.love: Nourish the relationship with care, ritual and attention, and give each other a proper place in your lives.
life.inner: Treat yourself as a vessel: steady your posture and commitments so that something larger can be cooked and offered through you.

question: What are you cooking for others, and is your vessel sound enough to carry it?

name: The Arousing
essence: A sudden shock jolts you awake. Fear is natural, but if you keep your center and learn from it, the alarm turns into relief and even laughter.

judgment.text: Thunder brings success. Thunder comes, and everyone trembles; afterward come laughter and easy talk. The thunder startles people for a hundred miles, yet the one leading the ceremony does not drop the ladle or the cup of sacred wine.
judgment.meaning: Thunder doubled: crash upon crash. Something sudden happens, an upset, a loss, a frightening piece of news, and it shakes everyone. The text does not tell you to be fearless. It accepts the fear and says it passes; afterward people laugh with relief. What matters is how you meet it. The image is of a priest in the middle of a sacrifice who does not spill the wine when the sky splits. Inner composure keeps you doing what is essential while the world shakes. A shock can also be a gift: it wakes you up, clears complacency, and starts new growth, the way spring thunder wakes the seeds. That is why the omen is success.

image.text: Thunder rolling again and again: the picture of Shock. The wise person, in fear and trembling, sets their life in order and examines themselves.
image.meaning: When thunder repeats, it gives you no chance to settle back into old habits. The wise person uses the fright well, turning it inward. What did this expose? Where was I careless? A shock you reflect on becomes a lesson; one you only flinch from repeats. Let the fear send you to put your house in order.

lines.text: Thunder comes, and you are terrified. Afterward come laughter and talk. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: This strong line at the bottom is the source of the whole hexagram, the first crack of thunder. It frightens you, and that fear makes you alert and careful. Because you respond to it seriously, things work out and you look back with relief, even humor. Do not be ashamed of being shaken. Let it sharpen you, and it ends well.

lines.text: Thunder comes with danger. You lose a vast store of treasure and climb the nine hills. Do not chase after it. In seven days you will get it back.
lines.meaning: The shock costs you something real, and the natural impulse is to scramble after what was lost. Instead, get to high ground: protect yourself, step out of the danger, and let the loss be. Chasing it now only puts you deeper in harm’s way. Seven days marks a full cycle; when the time turns, what truly belongs to you will return without your forcing it.

lines.text: Thunder leaves you dazed and distraught. If the shock moves you to act, there will be no disaster.
lines.meaning: You are weak and in the wrong place, and the blow leaves you stunned. Freezing is the danger. Use the shock as a push: get up and change what needs changing. If you move, even uncertainly, toward a better position, you escape harm. Paralysis is the only real threat here.

lines.text: Thunder gets stuck in the mud.
lines.meaning: The strong line is trapped between soft lines and loses its force, like a thunderclap swallowed by a swamp. You meant to respond boldly, but you are bogged down: by circumstances, by others’ inertia, or by your own heaviness. Energy spent struggling here sinks. Admit the stall, avoid thrashing, and look for firmer ground before you try again.

lines.text: Thunder goes and comes back, danger. But nothing is lost; there is still work to be done.
lines.meaning: Shocks keep coming, one after another, and you are the one at the center expected to lead. The good news is that if you hold to the middle way you lose nothing essential. Keep attending to the task in hand. Stay at your post, do the next thing, and the steady care you show will carry you through each wave.

lines.text: Thunder brings trembling and wild glances. Setting out now brings misfortune. If the shock has not reached you yet but has struck your neighbor, no mistake. Even so, there will be gossip among those close to you.
lines.meaning: At the end of the hexagram, the shock has spread and people are panicking, eyes darting. Do not rush into action in this state; it will go badly. If the blow is still falling on others and has not yet reached you, use the time to prepare calmly and you will be blameless. Expect some criticism from family or allies who think you should act; ignore it and keep your head.

life.work: A sudden disruption hits; stay calm, keep the essential work going, then review what it revealed and fix it.
life.love: An upset or revelation shakes the relationship; let the first fright pass before reacting, and talk honestly once you can laugh again.
life.inner: Let fear wake you rather than rule you; ask what this shock is showing you about your life.

question: What has this shock woken you up to?

name: Keeping Still
essence: Stop. Bring body and mind to rest, as still as a mountain, so that you act only when it is time to act and rest when it is time to rest.

judgment.text: Keeping still your back, you no longer feel the urges of your body. You walk through your courtyard and do not see the people there. No mistake.
judgment.meaning: Mountain doubled: stillness on stillness. The back is the one part of the body that has no senses facing the world, so keeping the back still means stopping where desire and reaction do not reach. You stop grasping at yourself, and even walking among others you are not pulled by them. This is not coldness or withdrawal; it is the calm of meditation, where the restless, wanting self quiets down. The commentaries add that stillness is about timing: stop when it is time to stop, move when it is time to move. Resting at the right point lets you see clearly. It brings no blame because you act from a still center instead of from impulse.

image.text: Mountains standing one beside the other: the picture of Keeping Still. The wise person does not let their thoughts go beyond their own situation.
image.meaning: Two mountains side by side, each solid and unmoving. Neither strays into the other’s ground. The wise person keeps their mind on what is actually theirs to handle, here and now, instead of drifting into worry, fantasy, or other people’s business. Thought that stays within its proper place becomes steady and clear, like a mountain.

lines.text: Keeping the toes still. No mistake. It pays to stay steady over the long run.
lines.meaning: The toes are where every step begins. Stopping here means not moving before you have thought, catching the impulse at the very start when it is easiest. This is the best time to hold back, and it costs you nothing. Make a habit of this pause. Lasting steadiness, not a single effort, is what makes it work.

lines.text: Keeping the calves still. You cannot save the one you are following, and your heart is not glad.
lines.meaning: The calves move when the thighs move; they cannot stop on their own. You are holding back, but someone you follow, a leader or a partner, is charging on, and you cannot stop them. You go along in body while disagreeing in heart. This is uncomfortable. Recognize what you can and cannot control. Keep your own stillness and accept that their momentum is not yours to halt.

lines.text: Keeping the hips still, stiffening the back. Danger. The heart is suffocating.
lines.meaning: This is forced stillness: clamping down on yourself at the waist, the joint between upper and lower body, until you are rigid. Suppression is not peace. Holding feelings or needs down by force builds pressure until the heart burns with it. If you are trying to be calm by strangling what you feel, stop. True stillness has to grow from inside, not be imposed with clenched muscles.

lines.text: Keeping the trunk still. No mistake.
lines.meaning: Now the stillness reaches the body itself, the chest and the self. You are able to quiet your own ego and anxieties, though not yet to bring calm to others. That is a sound and worthy step. Work on yourself first. You do no wrong by focusing here, even if it is not yet complete enlightenment.

lines.text: Keeping the jaws still. Words come in good order. Regret disappears.
lines.meaning: The jaws govern speech. Stillness here means not speaking carelessly: you choose words, pause before replying, and say only what is needed and in the right sequence. This is the ruler’s position; leaders especially should guard their tongues. When what you say comes from a calm mind, you will not have to take it back, and regret vanishes.

lines.text: Noble, wholehearted stillness. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: At the top of the mountain, stillness is no longer a practice but a character. You are calm all the way through, generous and settled, steady without strain. This is the fulfillment of the hexagram. It brings good fortune because a mind this quiet sees clearly and acts well. Let this composure be the ground you act from.

life.work: Pause before the next move; stop the busywork, focus only on what is yours to do, and resume when the time is clear.
life.love: Give yourself and the other person calm space; do not react on impulse or say what you will regret.
life.inner: Meditate, rest, or simply stop; let stillness grow naturally rather than forcing yourself to be calm.

question: Where do you need to stop, and what would you see if you did?

name: Development
essence: Lasting growth comes step by step, like a tree on a mountain or wild geese moving in stages toward the heights. Follow the proper sequence and don’t skip ahead.

judgment.text: Gradual progress: the maiden is given in marriage. Good fortune. It pays to stay steady and correct.
judgment.meaning: In ancient China a proper marriage unfolded through a long series of formal steps: proposal, gifts, choosing the date, and finally the bride going to her new home. Nothing could be rushed, and the slow process is what made the bond sound. This hexagram applies that pattern to any important development: a career, a relationship, a reputation, a skill. The lines follow a wild goose, a bird of fidelity that mates for life, as it moves from the shore to the rock, the plain, the tree, the hill and the heights. Each stage has its place. Progress that respects this order lasts; progress that jumps ahead does not. Good fortune, as long as you keep to the right way.

image.text: A tree on the mountain: the picture of Development. The wise person dwells in worthy character and so gradually improves the ways of the people.
image.meaning: A tree growing on a mountain grows slowly, rooted in hard ground and exposed to wind, but it becomes tall and visible for miles. Influence on others works the same way. The wise person does not preach or push; they live with integrity, and over time their example quietly changes the customs around them. Real change in people is never fast.

lines.text: The wild goose moves slowly toward the shore. The young one is in danger, and there is talk. No mistake.
lines.meaning: You are at the very start, inexperienced and without support, like a young bird at the water’s edge. People may criticize or doubt you. Do not be discouraged, and do not try to prove yourself by rushing. Cautious beginnings are exactly right. The talk is uncomfortable but it is no fault of yours, and the slow pace protects you.

lines.text: The wild goose moves slowly toward the great rock. It eats and drinks in peace and joy. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: You have reached secure footing, a solid rock above the water. Things are going well and you can enjoy them: food, company, a sense of being settled. This line in the centre corresponds with the ruler in line 5, so the support is real. Share what you have with others; contentment here is well earned and not mere indulgence.

lines.text: The wild goose moves slowly toward the high plain. The husband goes off and does not return. The wife conceives but does not bring the child to birth. Misfortune. It pays to guard against raiders.
lines.meaning: A water bird on a dry plain is out of its element. This line is strong at the top of the lower trigram, impatient to press on, and its haste breaks the gradual order. The images are of commitments abandoned and growth that does not come to term. Do not push into ground that is not yours or leave what you began. Instead, consolidate and defend what you have.

lines.text: The wild goose moves slowly toward the tree. Perhaps it finds a flat branch to rest on. No mistake.
lines.meaning: Geese have webbed feet and cannot grip branches, so a tree is an awkward place for them. You are in a situation that does not quite suit you. Look for a flat, stable spot: some practical arrangement that lets you rest safely for now. Being adaptable and modest will get you through without error.

lines.text: The wild goose moves slowly toward the summit. For three years the wife does not conceive. In the end nothing can stop it. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: You have risen high, but you feel cut off from the one you belong with, and for a long time your efforts bear no fruit. This line and line 2 are true partners, separated by obstacles in between. The barriers are temporary. Stay faithful to what you know is right and keep going; the union and its results will come, and nothing can prevent them.

lines.text: The wild goose moves slowly toward the cloud heights. Its feathers can be used in the sacred dance. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: The journey is complete. The goose has flown beyond the ordinary world, yet it leaves its feathers behind for the ritual dance, beautiful and useful to others. You have gone past the need for position or reward, and your life itself becomes an example. Whatever you have achieved, its real value is in what it gives back.

life.work: Advance step by step; build skill, trust and reputation patiently instead of trying to leap ahead.
life.love: Let the relationship develop in its own time, through each stage properly; commitment that is earned slowly is lasting.
life.inner: Trust slow growth; consistent small steps will change you more than dramatic resolutions.

question: What step are you trying to skip?

name: The Marrying Maiden
essence: You are entering a relationship or situation on unequal terms, moved more by desire than by proper arrangement. You cannot set the rules here; what helps is tact, modesty and an eye on how it will end.

judgment.text: The marrying maiden. Pushing forward brings misfortune. Nothing is favorable.
judgment.meaning: Gui Mei means a young girl going to her husband’s house, specifically as a junior wife who accompanied the principal bride, in a household where she had little say. The trigrams show it: a young lake, the youngest daughter, eager and joyful below, following an older thunder above, driven by attraction rather than by careful arrangement. The omen is harsh. This is not a position from which to take initiative. If you try to assert yourself, press demands, or treat a lesser role as an equal one, it goes badly. That is not a judgment on your worth. It describes a structure. Act with restraint and discretion, accept the limits of your place, and you can keep your dignity and still do good within it.

image.text: Thunder over the lake: the picture of the Marrying Maiden. The wise person understands what will fail by keeping the far end in view.
image.meaning: Thunder rolls and the lake’s surface stirs in response: feeling answers impulse. Such attractions are real but often fleeting. The wise person looks past the excitement of the beginning toward the lasting end. What will this bond be in ten years? By seeing which ties will endure and which will fray, you can enter relationships with open eyes and avoid the ones that are bound to break.

lines.text: The maiden marries as a secondary wife. A lame person who can still walk. Going forward brings good fortune.
lines.meaning: Your position is modest, and it limits you, like walking with a limp. But you can still move and be useful. If you accept the role without resentment and serve loyally and well, your strong character will earn you respect. Within these limits, going ahead turns out well.

lines.text: A one-eyed person who can still see. It pays to keep the steadiness of a solitary person.
lines.meaning: This strong line in the centre is paired with a weak partner above. You may be in a relationship or alliance where the other side lets you down, and your vision feels cut in half. Keep your own clarity and integrity anyway, like someone who lives quietly and faithfully on their own. Do not give up your loyalty or your standards because the other person falls short.

lines.text: The maiden marries in a lowly place, as someone waiting. She returns and goes as a secondary wife.
lines.meaning: You want something so much that you are tempted to accept terms beneath you just to get in. That trade rarely works. Settling for a degrading position out of eagerness leaves you worse off than waiting. Step back, keep your self-respect, and accept a modest role only if it is honest and honorable.

lines.text: The maiden lets the time for marriage pass. A late marriage comes in its own time.
lines.meaning: You are holding out rather than taking the first offer, and people may think you are missing your chance. But you are waiting for the right match on the right terms, and you are right to do so. This line is strong and principled. The delay is not loss. What is meant for you will come later, and it will be worth the wait.

lines.text: Sovereign Yi gives his daughter in marriage. The princess’s sleeves are not as fine as those of the secondary wife. The moon is almost full. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: A king’s daughter marrying below her rank does not dress to outshine anyone; her attendant is more lavishly clothed than she is. True nobility has no need for display. This ruler’s line is yielding and central. Whatever your status, enter humbly and let your worth show in conduct rather than in appearances. The moon not quite full means fulfillment without excess. Good fortune.

lines.text: The woman holds up a basket with no fruit in it. The man stabs the sheep, and no blood flows. Nothing is favorable.
lines.meaning: In the ancestral rite, the wife offers fruit and the husband sacrifices a lamb. Here the basket is empty and the sacrifice is bloodless: they go through the motions with nothing inside. This is a commitment that exists only in form, a relationship or project without real substance or feeling. It cannot succeed as it is. Be honest about what is missing rather than keep up an empty ritual.

life.work: You are in a junior or dependent role; do not overreach or demand equality you do not have, but serve well and protect your integrity.
life.love: A strong attraction or an unequal relationship: look clearly at where it leads and do not trade your dignity for closeness.
life.inner: Know the difference between impulse and commitment; ask how this will look at its end.

question: Seen from its end, what is this relationship really built on?

name: Abundance
essence: You are at a high point: full, bright, and powerful. Make the most of it like the sun at noon, without sorrow, knowing that every peak is followed by decline.

judgment.text: Abundance brings success. The king reaches it. Do not grieve. Be like the sun at midday.
judgment.meaning: Thunder above, lightning below: movement driven by clarity, energy and vision at full strength. This is the moment of greatest abundance, a harvest, a flourishing career, a full life. Only someone of real stature, the king, can reach and hold it. The text immediately adds: do not grieve. A wise person at the peak senses that, as the sun begins to sink just after noon, fullness must wane. Worrying about that only darkens the present. Instead, be like the noon sun, which shines on everything evenly and holds nothing back. Use this abundance generously and well while it lasts. That is the success.

image.text: Thunder and lightning arrive together: the picture of Abundance. The wise person decides lawsuits and carries out penalties.
image.meaning: Lightning lights up the whole scene and thunder follows with force. Clear insight together with decisive action. At a peak of power, the wise person uses that clarity to settle what is unresolved: making judgments, resolving disputes, dealing fairly with wrongs. Abundance is the time to see clearly and act firmly, not to put off hard decisions.

lines.text: You meet the partner who matches you. Even for ten days, there is no mistake. Going forward wins honor.
lines.meaning: This line meets line 4, both strong, of equal weight and purpose. Clarity at the bottom finds energy above. Working with an equal can be tense, but here it is right. Even a long partnership will not go wrong. Combine your strengths: one sees, the other moves. Go forward together and you will be recognized for it.

lines.text: The curtain is so thick that the stars of the Dipper can be seen at noon. Going on brings distrust and resentment. If you rouse sincerity, good fortune.
lines.meaning: At the height of abundance, something blots out the light, like an eclipse that brings out stars at midday. You see clearly, but the one above you, the weak ruler in line 5, is surrounded by shadows and cannot. Pushing your views on them will be met with suspicion. Instead, show steady sincerity; trust will slowly open the way and the light will return.

lines.text: The thicket is so dense that tiny stars can be seen at noon. You break your right arm. No mistake.
lines.meaning: The darkness is deeper now. You are capable and ready, but the one you would serve (line 6, weak and at the end) cannot use you. It is as if your strongest arm were broken and you cannot act at all. This is not your fault. Accept the inactivity without blaming yourself, and wait for a better time.

lines.text: The curtain is so thick that the Dipper can be seen at noon. You meet your equal, the ruler of your own kind. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: The shadows still hang over the top of the situation, but here, close to the ruler, you find a kindred spirit, line 1, with the same strength and drive. Together you can begin to dispel the darkness. Look for allies who share your purpose and combine your clarity with their energy. That partnership brings good fortune.

lines.text: Brilliance comes. There are blessings and praise. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: The ruler, yielding and modest, opens to talented people and lets them shine. Light arrives, and with it success and recognition. If you lead, be open to the abilities of those around you and give them room. If you are among the talented, step forward. Abundance flows from this mutual openness.

lines.text: The house is grand and abundant, but it shuts the family away. You peer through the gate, and it is silent, no one there. For three years you see no one. Misfortune.
lines.meaning: At the end of abundance comes isolation. Someone who has gathered wealth or status walls themselves in, too proud or too protective to let others near, and ends up alone in a fine, empty house. This goes badly. Do not let success cut you off. Open the doors, stay connected, and let people in while you still can.

life.work: You are at a peak; make the big decisions, settle open issues and share the gains, knowing this level will not last forever.
life.love: Enjoy the fullness of this time together and stay generous and open; do not let success or busyness isolate you.
life.inner: Shine fully now without fearing the decline that follows; noon is noon.

question: How would you use this abundance if you knew it would not last?

name: The Wanderer
essence: You are a traveler, a stranger in an unfamiliar place, without roots or standing. Move on gracefully: be modest and careful, keep to the right way, and do not overstay.

judgment.text: The Wanderer. Success in small things. For the traveler, steady correctness brings good fortune.
judgment.meaning: Fire on the mountain: a brush fire moves quickly across the slopes and does not stay anywhere for long. The wanderer has no home ground, no allies, no position. That might be literal travel, or a move, a new job, a temporary situation, or simply feeling like an outsider. In such conditions you cannot achieve great things, only small successes. What matters is your conduct. Be courteous, discreet, and careful who you trust. Don’t demand or show off, and don’t sink into self-pity. Keep your dignity and your principles intact, and you will be welcomed and passed along safely. A stranger who carries themselves well finds good fortune.

image.text: Fire on the mountain: the picture of the Wanderer. The wise person is clear-minded and careful in handing down penalties and does not let cases drag on.
image.meaning: The mountain stays still while the fire passes over it quickly: firmness beneath, clarity above. In the old texts, a prisoner should not be kept waiting in jail any more than a traveler should linger at the inn. Judge carefully and resolve matters swiftly. In your own life, don’t let disputes or grudges drag on. Deal with them clearly and move on.

lines.text: The wanderer fusses over petty things. In this way he brings disaster on himself.
lines.meaning: Weak and at the bottom, you are a traveler who is small-minded: haggling, fretting over trifles, or acting cheap and undignified. In a strange place, people judge you by such behavior and turn against you. That hurt is self-inflicted. Do not demean yourself. Even with little power, hold yourself with some dignity and generosity.

lines.text: The wanderer comes to an inn. He keeps his means close and gains a loyal young servant.
lines.meaning: In the centre of the lower trigram, you behave with balance and modesty, and things go well. You find a safe place to stay, you hold on to your resources, and you gain someone loyal to help you. Being decent and careful as a newcomer earns trust. Accept the help and protect what you have.

lines.text: The wanderer’s inn burns down. He loses his young servant. Holding on is dangerous.
lines.meaning: Strong at the top of the lower trigram, you act like you own the place: arrogant, demanding, interfering. As a stranger you have no standing for that, and the result is losing both your shelter and your help. Holding firm to this attitude is dangerous. Recognize that you are a guest, and treat those around you with respect.

lines.text: The wanderer finds a place to rest. He gains wealth and an axe. But his heart is not glad.
lines.meaning: You find a foothold and some means: money, tools, the ability to defend yourself. Yet it is not home. You are still on guard, still a stranger, and you know it. This unease is honest. Use what you have to stay safe, but do not mistake this halting place for where you belong.

lines.text: He shoots a pheasant. One arrow is lost. In the end, he wins praise and a position.
lines.meaning: The pheasant, a bird of the fire trigram, stands for beauty and refinement. You make a gesture of offering, perhaps a costly one, to win a place in this new world, and you lose a little in doing so. But it works. Your graciousness and skill are noticed, and the stranger is honored and given an office. A small sacrifice made with style opens doors.

lines.text: The bird’s nest burns. The wanderer laughs at first, then howls and weeps. He loses his ox through carelessness. Misfortune.
lines.meaning: At the top of the hexagram, the traveler has become careless and proud, laughing as though nothing could touch him. Then his nest, his base, is destroyed, and he loses the ox, the patient strength that carried him, without even noticing. This goes badly. When you are far from home, arrogance and inattention are costly. Stay humble and watch what you rely on.

life.work: In a temporary or unfamiliar role, keep a low profile, work carefully, aim for small wins and do not assume more authority than you have.
life.love: A relationship in transition or across distance: be considerate and clear, and do not take the other’s hospitality for granted.
life.inner: Feel like a stranger without losing your center; carry your home inside you.

question: Where are you a guest right now, and how would a good guest behave?

name: The Gentle
essence: Wind upon wind: influence that works by steady, quiet pressure rather than force. You get through by staying with something long enough, in a clear direction, until it gives way.

judgment.text: The gentle brings small success. It helps to have somewhere to go. It helps to see a person of real stature.
judgment.meaning: Wind gets into every crack, not by battering but by never stopping. Each trigram has one yielding line beneath two firm ones, so the picture is of something soft that bends and follows, and yet slowly reaches everywhere. That is why the success is called small: this is not the moment for dramatic breakthroughs, but for patient, consistent influence. Two conditions make it work. First, you need a direction; wind that blows every way at once moves nothing, so decide where you are going. Second, it helps to attach yourself to someone wiser or more established, a mentor, a sound institution, a clear principle, because gentleness without a worthy aim becomes mere drifting. Be adaptable in manner, firm in purpose, and keep at it.

image.text: Winds following one upon another: the gentle. So the wise person repeats their instructions and carries out their affairs.
image.meaning: One gust bends the grass; wind that keeps coming lays it flat. Lasting influence comes from repetition and follow-through, not one loud announcement. If you want something to take root in a team, a household, or your own habits, say it clearly, say it again, and then act on it so that words and deeds blow the same way. Steady, consistent signals change things that force cannot.

lines.text: Going forward, pulling back. The firmness of a soldier helps.
lines.meaning: Gentleness here has turned into dithering. You step toward a decision, then retreat, then step forward again, and nothing moves. The cure is a soldier’s discipline: pick a course and hold it. You do not need to become harsh; you need to stop second-guessing every step. Give yourself a deadline, commit to one direction, and let the yielding part of you serve that commitment instead of undermining it.

lines.text: Searching beneath the bed. Diviners and exorcists are brought in, in great numbers. Good fortune, no mistake.
lines.meaning: Something hidden is unsettling things, a buried motive, an old fear, a problem no one names, lurking low like something under the bed. The answer is to search it out thoroughly and bring in whatever help can expose it: people who see clearly, honest conversation, professional advice. A firm line in the center, you have the strength to look. Patient, methodical investigation drives the shadow out. This goes well, and you make no mistake by digging.

lines.text: Penetrating again and again. Humiliation.
lines.meaning: You keep pushing, reconsidering, probing, revising, and it has become anxious repetition rather than progress. A firm line forcing its way at the restless top of the lower trigram, you are trying to be gentle by effort, and it shows. Overthinking a decision or pressing someone over and over brings embarrassment. Stop circling. Make the call with what you already know, and accept that further analysis will not make you more certain.

lines.text: Regret disappears. In the hunt, three kinds of game are taken.
lines.meaning: A yielding line in the minister’s place, correctly positioned, serving well. Your earlier doubts dissolve because your gentle, attentive approach is now producing real results, and plenty of them. The three kinds of game were used for offerings, for guests and for the household: there is enough for every purpose. Modesty combined with active effort pays off here. Keep working steadily; the harvest is real.

lines.text: Steadiness brings good fortune. Regret disappears. Nothing that does not help. No good beginning, but a good end. Three days before the change, three days after the change. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: Here a firm, centered ruler sets out to correct something that started badly. You cannot redo the beginning, but you can make the ending sound. The key is the timing around the change: think carefully before you introduce it, and watch closely afterward to see how it lands and adjust. Three days before, three days after. Prepared, deliberate reform succeeds, and the earlier regret fades as the new course proves itself.

lines.text: Searching beneath the bed. He loses his money and his axe. Persisting brings misfortune.
lines.meaning: Searching has gone too far. Past the point of usefulness, you keep digging into hidden causes, suspicions and details, and in doing so you lose your resources and your axe, the power to decide and cut. Excessive accommodation and endless analysis have drained your strength. Continuing this way goes badly. Stop investigating, recover your ability to act, and make a decision even if it is imperfect.

life.work: Influence by consistency: a clear goal, repeated plainly and backed by follow-through, will move more than any single bold push.
life.love: Gentle persistence wins trust, but do not dissolve into endless accommodation; know what you want and say it kindly and clearly.
life.inner: Practice small, repeated steps in one direction, and notice when gentleness turns into indecision.

question: Where would steady, quiet pressure in one direction achieve what force has not?

name: The Joyous
essence: Lake upon lake: shared, open joy that refreshes everyone it touches. Real gladness rests on inner firmness and honesty; joy that is only seeking pleasure goes astray.

judgment.text: Joy. Success. It helps to stay true.
judgment.meaning: The lake gives pleasure: it reflects the sky, waters the land and draws people to its shore. Each trigram has firm lines within and a yielding line on top, which the tradition reads as strength inside and gentleness outside. That is the heart of real joy: steady and sincere at the core, warm and open in manner. Such joy wins people over without force; they follow willingly and even forget hardship. But the text adds a condition, stay true. Cheerfulness used to flatter, manipulate or escape leads to trouble. Keep your center honest, and let delight come from genuine connection, good work and shared purpose, and success follows naturally.

image.text: Lakes resting one beside the other: the joyous. So the wise person joins with friends to talk things through and practice together.
image.meaning: Two lakes linked together keep each other from drying up. In the same way, people who learn together refresh each other: talking through ideas, testing them in practice, correcting and encouraging one another. This is one of life’s steadiest joys. Seek companions in study and work, share what you know, and let honest discussion keep your understanding fresh and alive.

lines.text: Contented, harmonious joy. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: A firm line at the base, needing nothing from anyone. This is the simple, quiet gladness of being at ease with yourself and others, without wanting anything, without an angle. Because it is free of grasping, it has nothing to go wrong. Enjoy what is in front of you, be friendly without calculation, and let your contentment stand on its own. This goes well.

lines.text: Sincere joy. Good fortune. Regret disappears.
lines.meaning: A firm line in the center: joy grounded in honesty. You may be among people whose pleasures pull you toward compromise, but because your delight comes from integrity, you are not drawn off course. Any worry that you might be tempted or misread fades as your sincerity proves itself. Be genuinely glad, but stay true to yourself; that keeps you safe and well regarded.

lines.text: Joy that comes seeking. Misfortune.
lines.meaning: A weak line in an exposed place, turning outward for pleasure. This is joy that has to be fetched from outside: chasing distraction, approval, indulgence, anything to fill an inner emptiness. Such pleasures lead you around by the nose and leave you hollower than before. This goes badly. Turn back toward what nourishes you from within, and stop making your mood dependent on the next thing that arrives.

lines.text: Weighing up joys, not at peace. Once the affliction is cut away, there is gladness.
lines.meaning: You stand between two kinds of pleasure, one higher and one lower, the right path and the tempting one, and the indecision keeps you restless. As the minister near the ruler, this line must choose. Once you firmly reject what harms you, the unhealthy attachment, the shady offer, the easy indulgence, the unease lifts and real gladness follows. Make the choice cleanly.

lines.text: Trusting what strips you away. Danger.
lines.meaning: Even a strong, central position can be worn down. Here the ruler is close to the seductive top line, and gives trust to influences that erode it: flatterers, comfortable lies, people or habits that slowly hollow out your strength. Being in a good position makes you careless. This is dangerous. Notice what is quietly undermining you, and do not lend your confidence to it simply because it is pleasant.

lines.text: Drawn-out, enticing joy.
lines.meaning: At the top of the hexagram, pleasure has become an end in itself, prolonged and alluring. The text gives no omen, because the outcome depends on you: whether you are led along by enticement or see it for what it is. If you find yourself seducing or being seduced, stretching out enjoyment beyond its natural end, step back. Joy that must be drawn out has already lost its light.

life.work: Good spirits and open exchange move a team forward; keep the cheer honest and the substance real.
life.love: Delight in each other freely, but avoid flattery and pleasure-seeking that hollow out trust.
life.inner: Find the joy that needs nothing from outside, and be wary of the kind you have to chase.

question: Is the gladness you are seeking coming from within, or are you fetching it from outside?

name: Dispersion
essence: Wind blowing over water breaks up ice and scatters mist. What is frozen, divided or blocked can be dissolved, and what has scattered can be gathered again around something shared and sacred.

judgment.text: Dispersion. Success. The king goes to his temple. It helps to cross the great river. It helps to stay true.
judgment.meaning: Wind moves over water, and the hard surface breaks up; spring winds melt the ice. This hexagram is about dissolving what has hardened, whether selfishness, rigidity, resentment, or the walls between people, and also about gathering again what has scattered. The king going to the ancestral temple is the classic remedy: when hearts drift apart, bring them back to something larger than any one person, a shared value, a common memory, a purpose worth honoring. With that center restored, even great undertakings, the crossing of the great river, become possible. Stay true, though. Dispersion should loosen what is harmful, not dissolve your own principles. Let go of what divides, hold to what unites.

image.text: Wind moves over the water: dispersion. So the ancient kings made offerings to the Lord on High and built temples.
image.meaning: When people scatter like ripples blown across a lake, something is needed to draw them back together. The ancient rulers answered with worship and shared ritual: a place and practice that reminded everyone what they belonged to. For you this may be a common purpose, a family tradition, a moment of reverence or gratitude. Build places, rituals and habits that reconnect people to what matters beyond themselves.

lines.text: He brings help with the strength of a horse. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: At the very beginning of a falling-apart, quick, strong help can prevent much worse. A weak line at the base cannot do it alone, so it relies on a strong ally, the firm line above it, the horse. Do not wait for division or misunderstanding to set hard; act at once and use whatever capable support you can find. Early, vigorous action dissolves the problem while it is still small. This goes well.

lines.text: In the midst of dispersion he hurries to his support. Regret disappears.
lines.meaning: When things are scattering around you, run to what steadies you, like reaching for a solid bench to lean on. That may be a trusted friend, a core principle, a calm practice, or the people who hold you up. A firm line fallen into the middle of danger, you need grounding before you can do anything else. Once you have found it, the regret and unease dissolve.

lines.text: He dissolves his self. No regret.
lines.meaning: Here what gets dispersed is your own ego: self-concern, pride, the need to be right. This is a sacrifice of sorts, but a healthy one. Turning your attention to a larger task or to others frees you from a cramped, anxious selfhood. You will not regret it. Ask what you would do if your own standing did not matter, and do that.

lines.text: He dissolves his faction. Supreme good fortune. Dispersion leads to gathering, a hill. Ordinary people do not think of this.
lines.meaning: The minister breaks up the cliques and small loyalties around him, and that very act gathers people into something larger, a great hill rising from scattered earth. It takes vision to see that letting go of your circle, your group interests or your partisan camp can create a wider unity. Most people cling to their faction. If you put the whole first, the outcome is excellent.

lines.text: His great cries dissolve things, like sweat breaking out. He disperses the royal stores. The king abides without mistake.
lines.meaning: In a crisis the ruler issues a clear, powerful call that spreads through everyone, the way sweat breaks a fever, and even shares out the royal stores. A strong, central leader can unite scattered people with a decisive idea and real generosity. If you are in charge, now is the time for a clear message and open hands. Leading from that center, you make no mistake.

lines.text: He disperses his blood. Going away, keeping far off, getting out: no mistake.
lines.meaning: At the top, beyond the danger, the task is to dissolve the threat of harm, the bloodshed, the conflict, by distancing yourself from it. Sometimes the wisest way through is to remove yourself and those you love from a dangerous situation entirely. Leaving is not cowardice here; it ends the injury. Step away from what wounds you. No mistake.

life.work: Break up rigid silos and personal agendas by rallying people around a shared purpose larger than any one of them.
life.love: Melt resentment and coldness early, before it freezes; return together to what you both value.
life.inner: Loosen the grip of the self and let something larger steady you.

question: What hardness in you, or between you and others, is ready to be dissolved, and what could you gather around instead?

name: Limitation
essence: A lake can hold only so much water. Healthy limits give life shape and strength, but limits that become harsh and bitter cannot last.

judgment.text: Limitation. Success. Bitter limits should not be held to rigidly.
judgment.meaning: Water above a lake: the lake is useful because it has banks. Pour in too much and it overflows; give it no edge and it spreads into a marsh. Limits are what make things work, like a budget, a schedule, a promise, a measured diet, the joints that divide bamboo into strong sections. The Chinese name means exactly those joints. So limitation brings success. Yet the text adds a warning: limits so severe that they grind people down, yourself included, cannot be sustained. Bitter restriction breeds rebellion or collapse. The art is to set limits that are firm yet bearable, that give structure without strangling. Find the right measure, then keep it.

image.text: Water over the lake: limitation. So the wise person sets out number and measure, and examines what true virtue and right conduct are.
image.meaning: The lake can only hold so much; beyond that it spills. The wise person studies proportion: how much, how often, how far. Setting clear standards of quantity and measure, and reflecting on what good conduct actually requires, gives a life or a community dependable shape. Decide what is enough in your spending, your work, your commitments, and let those limits express your values rather than arbitrary rules.

lines.text: Not going out past the inner door and courtyard. No mistake.
lines.meaning: At the beginning, the right limit is to stay home. Conditions outside are not yet favorable, and you are not ready. Keep your counsel, contain your plans, and do not speak or move before the time. The tradition links this to discretion: words leaked too early can undo an undertaking. Holding back now is no mistake; it protects what you are preparing.

lines.text: Not going out past the outer gate and courtyard. Misfortune.
lines.meaning: Now the moment to act has come, and you still hold back. What was prudence at the first line has become timidity. A firm line in the center, you have the capacity, but you cling to safety while the opening passes. This goes badly. Limits are meant to serve timing, not replace it. When the gate is open, walk through.

lines.text: Those who do not keep limits will have to lament. No one else to blame.
lines.meaning: A weak line in a strong place, sitting at the edge of the lake: overindulgence spilling over. If you spend, eat, promise or take beyond your measure, you will end up sighing about it. The text says the fault is no one else’s. The upside is that recognizing this yourself is the first step to correcting it. Own it, and set the limit now.

lines.text: Contented limitation. Success.
lines.meaning: Limits accepted willingly and naturally, like water settling into its channel. The minister, yielding and correctly placed, works easily within the ruler’s measure. When you keep limits because you see their sense, not because they are forced on you, they cost little energy and bring steady success. Find the structure that fits you and rest in it.

lines.text: Sweet limitation. Good fortune. Going forward wins respect.
lines.meaning: The ruler, firm and central, sets limits first on himself, and makes them agreeable rather than oppressive. Limits you keep personally before asking them of others feel sweet, not bitter, and people follow gladly. If you lead, model the discipline you want. Acting from this example brings good fortune, and going forward this way earns real respect.

lines.text: Bitter limitation. Persisting brings misfortune. Regret disappears.
lines.meaning: At the extreme, limits have become harsh and punishing, severe asceticism, rigid control, rules that crush. Insisting on this goes badly over time; neither you nor others can sustain it. Yet the line also says regret fades: in a real emergency, severe measures may briefly be what saves you. Use harshness only as a short-term remedy, and do not make a way of life of it.

life.work: Set clear budgets, scopes and deadlines that are firm but humane; keep them yourself first.
life.love: Good boundaries make closeness possible; just make sure they protect the relationship rather than punish it.
life.inner: Know your measure, and ask whether your self-discipline feels sweet or bitter.

question: Which limit in your life gives you strength, and which has become bitter and needs to be eased?

name: Inner Truth
essence: Wind over the lake, stirring the water to its depths. Sincerity so real that it reaches even the least receptive creatures, and moves the world from within.

judgment.text: Inner truth. Pigs and fishes. Good fortune. It helps to cross the great river. It helps to stay true.
judgment.meaning: The hexagram looks like an open heart: two yielding lines in the middle, held by firm lines above and below. Empty at the center, yet strong in the middle of each trigram, this is the picture of sincerity: free of agenda inside, solid in character. Pigs and fishes are the most unresponsive of creatures, or the humblest of offerings, and the text says real sincerity reaches even them. When your truthfulness is that deep, it can move people who seem impossible to influence, and carry you through the hardest crossings. But sincerity must be to what is right, so the text adds: stay true. Understand others from the inside, as they are, and let that honest understanding guide you.

image.text: Wind over the lake: inner truth. So the wise person deliberates carefully over legal cases and delays executions.
image.meaning: Wind stirs the water, reaching down into what is hidden. Similarly, the wise person seeks to understand the inner reality of others, especially when judging them. Before condemning, listen; look for the motive and circumstance; give mercy room. When you must evaluate someone, at work or at home, slow down and let real understanding, not quick verdicts, shape what you do.

lines.text: Being ready and settled brings good fortune. If there is another, there is no peace.
lines.meaning: At the beginning, truth comes from inner preparedness and steadiness, being grounded in yourself. If you rely on hidden attachments, side deals or another person to prop you up, you lose your peace. Keep your trust simple and undivided. Settle what you believe and act from it. That steadiness brings good fortune; split loyalties bring unrest.

lines.text: A crane calls from the shade. Its young one answers. I have a fine cup of wine; I will share it with you.
lines.meaning: Real sincerity needs no stage. The crane calls unseen, and its young hears and answers; true feeling reaches those attuned to it, however hidden. A firm, central line, you do not need to perform or persuade. Speak honestly, share what is good, and the right people will respond. Influence of this kind spreads quietly and naturally, like an offered cup among friends.

lines.text: He finds a counterpart. Now he drums, now he stops. Now he weeps, now he sings.
lines.meaning: Your center of gravity sits in someone else. Your moods swing with them, up, down, at war, at peace, because a weak line in the wrong place relies on its correspondence for its sense of itself. This can be the giddy instability of love or rivalry. It is not marked as disaster, but it is exhausting. Find your own steadiness so your joy and sorrow are not entirely on loan.

lines.text: The moon nearly full. One horse of the pair goes off. No mistake.
lines.meaning: Near its fullest light, at the height of influence, the minister turns humbly toward the ruler and away from the old companion, one horse of the team leaving its partner. Sometimes faithfulness to a higher purpose means stepping away from a former alliance or faction. Like the moon just short of full, keep a little modesty. Choosing this way is no mistake.

lines.text: He holds truth that binds others together. No mistake.
lines.meaning: The ruler, firm and central, is so trustworthy that it links people together as firmly as a rope. Your sincerity holds the group, the team or the family together. Others rely on you because your words and actions match. Lead from that inner consistency and the bonds hold. No mistake.

lines.text: The sound of wings rising to heaven. Persisting brings misfortune.
lines.meaning: A barnyard bird that tries to fly to heaven: its cry and flapping rise, but it cannot. At the top, sincerity has become mere sound, words outrunning substance, faith turned to claim. Keep insisting, and it goes badly. Check whether what you are proclaiming is still backed by reality, and bring your words back down to what you can truly carry.

life.work: Influence comes from genuine trustworthiness and understanding people as they really are, not from clever persuasion.
life.love: Speak from the heart without performance; those truly attuned will answer.
life.inner: Empty yourself of agenda and stay centered, so your sincerity is both open and solid.

question: Where is your influence built on genuine trust, and where are your words running ahead of what you really mean?

name: Small Exceeding
essence: Thunder on the mountain: a time when only small things can be done, and you should exceed in care, humility and frugality rather than ambition. The bird should not fly high.

judgment.text: Small exceeding. Success. It helps to stay true. Small things can be done; great things cannot. The flying bird leaves its message: it is not good to climb, it is good to stay low. Great good fortune.
judgment.meaning: Four yielding lines surround two firm ones in the middle, the picture of a bird, body inside, wings spread. The weak outnumber the strong, so this is not a time for great deeds. Instead you may go a little beyond the ordinary in small ways: be more careful, more modest, more attentive than usual. The flying bird is the warning image. If it soars, it is exposed and finds no resting place; if it stays near the ground, it is safe. Do not reach for bold expansion, a grand plan or a risky leap. Attend to details, do modest things well, and the outcome is excellent. Overreaching brings the trouble the lines describe.

image.text: Thunder on the mountain: small exceeding. So the wise person goes a little beyond in reverence when acting, in grief when mourning, in thrift when spending.
image.meaning: Thunder heard from the mountaintop sounds smaller than in the plain. The lesson is to lean slightly toward the humble side. Be a bit more respectful than expected, more sincere in sorrow than in show, more careful with money than strictly needed. Not large gestures, but small, deliberate excesses of modesty that keep you grounded and safe.

lines.text: The bird flies, and meets misfortune.
lines.meaning: At the very start, you want to take off before you have grown your wings. This weak line corresponds with the strong fourth line above and feels drawn upward. Leaping too early brings misfortune here. Stay in the nest a while longer. Do the groundwork, build experience, wait until you are ready. Ambition at this stage gets you hurt.

lines.text: She passes her grandfather and meets her grandmother. She does not reach the prince, but meets his minister. No mistake.
lines.meaning: You do not get straight to the top, but meet someone at the right level, the grandmother instead of the grandfather, the minister instead of the prince. Yielding and central, this line accepts going through proper channels rather than overreaching. That is exactly right now. Work with the people and the access you actually have, show respect, and progress comes. No mistake.

lines.text: If you do not take extra precautions, someone may come from behind and strike you. Misfortune.
lines.meaning: A strong line in a strong place, at the top of the lower trigram, confident, perhaps too confident. Danger comes from an angle you are not watching, a quiet opponent, an overlooked risk, a backstabber. If you neglect precautions out of pride, you will be hurt. This goes badly unless you guard yourself. Check your blind spots and do not assume goodwill everywhere.

lines.text: No mistake. He meets it without overstepping. Going forward is dangerous; you must be on guard. Do not act. Stay steady for the long run.
lines.meaning: A strong line in a yielding place, holding itself back: wise restraint. You meet the situation as it is, without pushing past your bounds. But if you press forward now, danger awaits. Keep your guard up and do not take the initiative. This is not a time to force outcomes; be consistent, patient and watchful until conditions change.

lines.text: Dense clouds but no rain, from our western lands. The prince shoots and takes the one in the cave.
lines.meaning: Clouds gather but rain does not fall: the potential is there, but the ruler, a yielding line, cannot accomplish great things alone. So he reaches for help, bringing out a capable person hidden in obscurity, like a hunter drawing game from its cave. Look for able, overlooked people and draw them in. Small, well-chosen steps of this kind prepare the rain that will come.

lines.text: He does not meet it, he passes far beyond. The flying bird is caught in the net. Misfortune. This is called disaster and injury.
lines.meaning: At the top, the bird has flown much too high and too far, exceeding every bound, and is caught. You overshoot the mark, ignore the limits, and the result is real calamity, both bad luck and harm you bring on yourself. If you are pushing past every warning, stop. Come back down, before the consequences catch you.

life.work: Do small things meticulously and avoid big leaps; this is not the time to expand or take risks.
life.love: Little acts of respect and care matter more now than grand gestures.
life.inner: Practice a slight excess of humility, carefulness and thrift, and resist the urge to soar.

question: Where are you trying to fly too high, when staying low and doing small things well would serve you better?

name: After Completion
essence: Water above fire: everything is in its place, the crossing is done. But order is at its most fragile just after it is achieved, so careful vigilance is needed to keep it.

judgment.text: After completion. Success in small matters. It helps to stay true. Good fortune at the beginning, disorder at the end.
judgment.meaning: This is the only hexagram where every line is in its proper place: firm lines in firm places, yielding in yielding, each matched with its partner. Water above fire, like a pot on the stove, things work together. The goal has been reached. Yet the text is sober. Only small successes remain; the great work is done. And it warns that what begins well tends to slide into disorder. Perfect balance does not last by itself: the water may boil over or put out the fire. After the project is delivered, the house bought, the relationship settled, the danger is complacency. Stay attentive to details, maintain what works, and do not assume order will keep itself.

image.text: Water over fire: after completion. So the wise person thinks ahead to trouble and guards against it in advance.
image.meaning: A pot of water over the flame is useful, but it needs watching: too much heat and it boils dry or spills onto the fire. Things that are in balance require tending. Anticipate what could go wrong in your current success, a bottleneck, a slow decline, a neglected relationship, and take precautions now, while things are good. Prevention costs little compared with repair.

lines.text: He brakes his wheels. He gets his tail wet. No mistake.
lines.meaning: Just after success everyone is rushing on, and you hold back, like braking a cart or a fox that has only wet its tail and pulls back from the river. Restraint at the start of a new phase saves you from overshooting. A little setback or hesitation now is no harm. Slow down, consolidate, and do not chase the momentum. No mistake.

lines.text: The woman loses the curtain of her carriage. Do not chase after it. On the seventh day you will get it back.
lines.meaning: You lose something that gave you standing or protection, a recognition, a title, a cover, and you are tempted to run after it. Do not. Yielding and centered, correct in conduct, you will be acknowledged again in time. Seven days is a full cycle: what belongs to you returns by itself. Keep your conduct sound and wait; pursuit would only cost you dignity.

lines.text: The High Ancestor attacks the Demon Land. After three years he conquers it. Small people must not be employed.
lines.meaning: Even after completion, a large undertaking may be needed, like the great king’s long campaign against the barbarian lands. It is possible, but it takes years, exhausts resources, and must be led by capable people with integrity. Short-sighted or self-serving helpers would wreck it. If you take on a major venture now, count the full cost and choose your people with great care.

lines.text: The finest silks turn to rags. Be on guard all day long.
lines.meaning: Good clothes become rags; the boat has leaks that must be stuffed with old cloth. Small signs of decay are appearing in a successful situation. Do not ignore them. Stay alert throughout the day, patch what is wearing thin, and watch for trouble before it becomes serious. Constant, modest vigilance is the right attitude now.

lines.text: The neighbor in the east slaughters an ox, but this does not equal the neighbor in the west and his small offering, who truly receives the blessing.
lines.meaning: Lavish display at the height of success matters less than a modest offering made sincerely. The grand gesture, the big celebration, the impressive show, does not win real blessing; heartfelt simplicity does. As a strong ruler in the center, you have the means for extravagance. Choose sincerity instead. What counts is the spirit, not the size.

lines.text: He gets his head wet. Danger.
lines.meaning: At the end, the one who completed the crossing turns back to look, or keeps going into the water, and is in over his head. Lingering over past success or pushing too far after completion puts you in danger. Do not keep looking back at what you have achieved, and do not wade on beyond the goal. Recognize that the crossing is over and move on with care.

life.work: After a launch or milestone, shift to maintenance and risk management; complacency is the main threat.
life.love: Settled relationships still need daily attention; small repairs now prevent large breakdowns later.
life.inner: Enjoy what has been achieved, but keep a quiet watchfulness.

question: Now that something has come together, what small signs of decay are you tempted to overlook?

name: Before Completion
essence: Fire above water: everything is out of place, but the possibility of order is present. You are nearly across, so take great care in the final stretch.

judgment.text: Before completion. Success. The little fox has almost crossed the river, then wets its tail. Nothing helps.
judgment.meaning: Here every line is out of its proper place, yet each still corresponds with its partner. Fire rising, water sinking: they move apart. It is a time of transition, of chaos with the seeds of order. The image is the young fox crossing an icy river. Older foxes go cautiously, listening for cracks; the young one hurries, and just short of the far bank gets its tail wet and fails. Success is promised because the situation can be resolved, but only by steady caution through to the end. Many efforts collapse in the last stretch, through impatience or overconfidence. Do not relax because the goal is in sight. Keep testing the ice.

image.text: Fire above water: before completion. So the wise person carefully distinguishes things, so that each finds its proper place.
image.meaning: Fire belongs above and water below; when they are where they naturally go, they do not interact, and nothing happens. Order comes from sorting things out patiently: understanding the nature of each element in a situation, each person in a team, each part of a problem, and putting it where it belongs. Before bringing things together, see clearly what each one is.

lines.text: He gets his tail wet. Humiliation.
lines.meaning: At the very start you rush into the crossing without knowing how deep the water is, and get wet at once. A weak line at the bottom, you lack the strength and experience to push through now. Acting this early leads to embarrassment. Do not be impatient. Learn the situation, prepare, and wait until you can actually make it across.

lines.text: He brakes his wheels. Staying steady brings good fortune.
lines.meaning: A strong line in the center holds back on purpose, braking the cart. You have the power to move, but the time is not quite right, and you serve the yielding ruler above by waiting. Patient restraint combined with readiness brings good fortune. Keep your strength in reserve and stay steady; your moment is coming.

lines.text: Before completion, setting out to attack brings misfortune. It helps to cross the great river.
lines.meaning: You are not yet able to finish the job by force, and pushing ahead aggressively would go badly. Yet the text also says it helps to cross the great river. The tradition reconciles this: do not charge in alone, but undertake the crossing with help, change your approach, or move into a new situation altogether. Avoid direct confrontation; seek a different route or strong allies.

lines.text: Staying steady brings good fortune. Regret disappears. With thunderous force he attacks the Demon Land. For three years there are rewards from the great kingdom.
lines.meaning: Now is the time for decisive effort. Hesitation and regret fall away. Like a long campaign against a stubborn foe, real struggle is required, and it takes sustained energy, three years of work, before the reward comes. But the reward is real and recognized. Commit fully to the hard part of the transition, and keep going until it is done.

lines.text: Staying steady brings good fortune. No regret. The light of the noble one is true. Good fortune.
lines.meaning: The ruler, yielding and centered, at the height of the bright trigram: the crossing has been made, and it shines. Your modesty and openness have drawn capable people to you, and their help has brought success. This is the clear light of integrity that others can trust. No regret. Keep that humility and truthfulness, and good fortune continues.

lines.text: Drinking wine with confidence. No mistake. But if he gets his head wet, he loses it.
lines.meaning: Completion is near, and it is right to celebrate with trust in the future. No mistake in that. But if celebration turns to excess, drinking until your head is in the water, you lose the very confidence and good sense that brought you here. Enjoy the success, with measure. Overindulgence at the end can undo what was achieved.

life.work: You are close to delivering; this is when diligence matters most, so check details and do not rush the finish.
life.love: A relationship in transition needs patience; sort out what each of you needs before trying to settle everything.
life.inner: Hold the hope of completion lightly, and keep your care steady to the very end.

question: Where are you almost across, and what would it take to finish with the same care you started with?
